Always structure your Ansible content into roles and collections. Each role or module must focus on a single, well-defined task. Avoid monolithic roles. Create dedicated `_info` or `_facts` modules/tasks for gathering information.

Enforce strict YAML formatting. All YAML files must begin with `---`. Use two spaces for indentation, never tabs. Quote strings only when necessary; prefer single quotes. Use exactly one space after a colon in key-value pairs. Always use the structured map style for module parameters, not the legacy `key=value` style. Quote octal modes. Standardize on `true`/`false`.

Adopt consistent `snake_case` naming. Prefix role names with the collection namespace.

Write idempotent tasks. Favor declarative modules over imperative `command` or `shell`. Always use `atomic_move` (implicitly via `copy`, `template` modules) for file modifications to prevent data corruption. Manage configurations with templates and structured variables. Define role variables in `defaults/main.yml` (overridable) and `vars/main.yml` (not overridable by inventory/extra-vars). Prefer inventory variables for host-specific data.

Disable fact gathering (`gather_facts: false`) if not explicitly needed. Use `setup` or `ansible.builtin.gather_facts` selectively. Leverage Ansible's parallelism by default, but be mindful of resource constraints. Use `fail_json` (in custom modules) or `ansible.builtin.fail` for clear error messages. Avoid raw tracebacks. Use `ansible.builtin.debug` with verbosity levels for controlled output.

Run `ansible-lint` on every pull request. Use `ansible-test` for unit and integration testing of custom modules and roles.
`ansible-test sanity -
